newsitem.title: USA: New drug, surgeries highlight U.S. heart meeting.
newsitem.headline: New drug, surgeries highlight U.S. heart meeting.

text.p: A drug that could replace aspirin for heart patients and a growing interest in new, minimally invasive surgical techniques were the highlights of the annual American Heart Association meeting, which ended in New Orleans on Wednesday.

Whether the new drug -- being developed by Sanofi SA and Bristol-Myers Squibb Co -- will eventually take the place of aspirin in many heart patients' regimens may hinge on its cost, pharmaceutical analysts said. The key is the cost of the treatment versus any medical savings realized from its use.

A study unveiled on Wednesday showed that patients receiving the drug, called clopidogrel, reduced their risk of stroke, heart attack and death due to cardiovascular problems by 8.7 percent compared with those treated with aspirin, researchers said.

Such an improvement could reduce the number of strokes, heart attacks or cardiovascular-related deaths by about 100,000 a year. Clopidogrel also did not lead to the kind of stomach bleeding sometimes caused by aspirin.

Still, the data may not be convincing enough for the drug to gain widespread use by cost-conscious health maintenance organizations in the United States and government health programs elsewhere, analysts said.
Ken Kulju, an analyst with UBS Securities, cited the once-a-day dosing and the absence of major side effects as potential selling points of clopidogrel.
He said he thought the drug could generate higher sales than another Sanofi drug, ticlopidine or Ticlid, which he listed as having $750 million in annual worldwide sales.
Clopidogrel is a derivative of ticlopidine, which is about 10 percent more effective than aspirin but causes side effects including rashes and diarrhea.

Also garnering attention at the association's meeting were new surgical techniques that avoid cracking open the chest to gain access to the heart for bypass and valve repairs. That minimizes the subsequent pain and cuts hospital costs.
Companies working on devices for the procedures include Heartport Inc, CardioThoracic Systems Inc, Medtronic and U.S. Surgical Corp.

Studies were also presented showing that small doses of radiation could help prevent the reclosure of blood vessels after angioplasty. Companies working in that field include Novoste Corp and Isostent Inc.

Centocor Inc's and Eli Lilly and Co's blood-clot fighting drug ReoPro also gained broad exposure at the meeting. Study results were presented that showed the drug maintained its effect in reducing deaths and heart attacks in angioplasty patients six months after the procedure.
